summary: SLH-DSA is a stateless hash-based signature algorithm. This RFC specifies how to use it with the Cryptographic Message Syntax, and provides the algorithm identifier and public key syntax.

eli5.summary: A new signing method uses only scrambling functions. This says how to use it for signed messages and files.

subtitle: How to sign CMS messages with SLH-DSA, a post-quantum signature built only from hash functions.

tldr.problem: Widely used signature algorithms such as RSA, DSA, ECDSA and EdDSA could be broken if a cryptographically relevant quantum computer is ever built, so signed messages need a post-quantum option.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 9814 defines twelve algorithm identifiers for SLH-DSA, a stateless hash-based signature, and says how to use it in the CMS signed-data content type, in pure mode with an empty context string.
tldr.outcome: CMS signers and verifiers get a post-quantum signature that does not need the signer to keep state, along with rules for public key encoding, hash choices and signed attributes.

today: RFC 9814 is a Proposed Standard from July 2025. The unit metadata shows it is not obsoleted or updated by any other RFC.

sections.title: What the RFC Specifies
sections.content:
This RFC gives the conventions for using the SLH-DSA hash-based signature algorithm (from NIST FIPS 205) with the Cryptographic Message Syntax (RFC 5652) signed-data content type. CMS values are generated with ASN.1 using the Basic and Distinguished Encoding Rules.

SLH-DSA offers a pure mode and a pre-hash mode, and its signature operations take a context string of at most 255 bytes that is empty by default. This document only specifies pure mode with an empty context string for CMS signed-data.

There are three security levels, chosen to give 128, 192 and 256 bits of security, and each has its own algorithm identifiers.
sections.eli5: This is the instruction sheet for putting a new kind of unforgeable signature on digital envelopes. It picks one simple way of doing it and leaves the other ways out.

sections.title: Why a Hash-Based Signature
sections.content:
The motivation is recent advances in cryptanalysis and in quantum computers. If Cryptographically Relevant Quantum Computers (CRQCs) are ever built, they will be able to break many public key systems in use now, including RSA, DSA, ECDSA and EdDSA. A Post-Quantum Cryptosystem is secure against quantum computers that have more than a trivial number of qubits.

The RFC says it is open to conjecture when such machines will exist, but it is prudent to use algorithms that stay secure if one is invented. SLH-DSA is a post-quantum signature algorithm.

It is also stateless. Other hash-based schemes such as HSS/LMS (RFC 8554) and XMSS (RFC 8391) are stateful. With no state for the signer to keep, SLH-DSA is much less fragile.
sections.eli5: Today's locks might be picked by a future super-machine. This lock is made from a different kind of puzzle, and it does not need you to remember how many times you used it.

sections.title: How SLH-DSA Works in Brief
sections.content:
SLH-DSA combines a few-time signature construction called FORS (Forest of Random Subsets) with a hypertree. FORS signs the message, and its tree roots are hashed together into a FORS root. That root is signed by a one-time scheme called WOTS+, whose public keys form the leaves of layers of Merkle subtrees. Each subtree root is signed by the layer above, until the top subtree forms the hypertree root, which the verifier trusts.

A signature holds a randomization string, the FORS signature, the WOTS+ signature in each layer and the path to each subtree root. Verification succeeds only if everything hashes up to the pre-trusted hypertree root.

Stateful schemes lose their security if a WOTS+ key is ever reused. In SLH-DSA, reusing a key to sign two different messages lowers security but does not collapse it. The design signs up to 2^64 messages, and the parameters give security at least as strong as a generic block cipher of 128, 192 or 256 bits.
sections.eli5: It is like a family tree of locks where each lock vouches for the ones below it, and everybody trusts the lock at the very top. To fake a signature you would have to fake the whole chain.

sections.title: Algorithm Identifiers and Keys
sections.content:
An SLH-DSA public key MUST use one of twelve id-slh-dsa object identifiers. The name encodes the hash family (SHA2 or SHAKE), the security level (128, 192 or 256) and the variant: s for small or f for fast. For example, id-slh-dsa-shake-256s means the 256-bit level, the small version, with SHAKE256. The parameters field of the AlgorithmIdentifier MUST be absent.

In an X.509 certificate the key usage extension MAY contain digitalSignature, nonRepudiation, keyCertSign and cRLSign, and MUST NOT contain other values.

Keys have no extra ASN.1 wrapping inside a SubjectPublicKeyInfo or a PrivateKeyInfo. Outside those structures, a public key can be carried as an OCTET STRING of size 32, 48 or 64 bytes, and a private key as one of size 64, 96 or 128 bytes. The object identifiers all sit under the NIST signature algorithm arc, numbered 20 through 31.
sections.eli5: Each version of the signature has its own name tag that says how strong it is, which scrambling machine it uses, and whether it is built to be small or fast.

sections.title: Signed-Data Conventions
sections.content:
Without signed attributes, the pure-mode signature is computed over the content. With signed attributes present, a hash SHOULD be computed over the DER-encoded signed attributes using the same hash function as the SLH-DSA tree. The attributes MUST include a content-type attribute and a message-digest attribute, and the signature covers the DER encoding of the whole attribute set. Signing attributes can improve performance when the content is large.

In the SignerInfo, the digestAlgorithm MUST identify a one-way hash function. When signed attributes are present, it MUST produce a hash at least twice the size of the one used in the tree, to keep collision resistance. When they are absent, it SHOULD match the tree hash but plays no role, and signers MAY always choose SHA-256 to help legacy implementations.

The signatureAlgorithm MUST be one of the twelve identifiers with absent parameters. Verification MUST check that the signatureAlgorithm names SLH-DSA parameters consistent with the public key.
sections.eli5: The signer can either sign the whole letter or sign a short summary card of it. The summary card is quicker for big letters, and it must be made with a strong enough summarizer.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Implementations MUST protect private keys, because compromise lets an attacker forge signatures. Each key pair MUST be generated independently of the others in the hypertree, and a tree MUST NOT be used for more than 2^64 signing operations.

Key generation relies on random numbers, and a weak generator can leave little or no security, so the RFC points to RFC 4086 for guidance. To resist algorithm-substitution attacks, the CMSAlgorithmProtection attribute from RFC 6211 SHOULD be included in signed attributes.

Implementers may add fault-attack countermeasures. Checking a signature before releasing it is typical, but it is not effective for SLH-DSA. Replicating the signing process MAY help, although signing is already slow. They may also consider protections against passive power and emissions side-channel attacks.
sections.eli5: Guard your secret stamp, and make sure you pick it using real dice rolls, not predictable ones. Do not use one stamp-set more than its limit.

sections.title: Operational Considerations
sections.content:
If signing runs in a hardware device such as a Hardware Security Module, signed attributes mean only the small attribute set goes to the device, not the full content. This gives interface characteristics similar to pre-hash mode, which is why pre-hash mode is not specified for CMS SignedData. A pre-hash signature always differs from a pure-mode signature, even for the same content.

In pure mode, a recipient cannot verify a message without signed attributes in a single pass over the content. So implementers SHOULD include signed attributes in any SignerInfo using SLH-DSA, which lets recipients using stream-based APIs avoid keeping the content in memory.

On the IANA side, an object identifier for the ASN.1 module (identifier 81, id-mod-slh-dsa-2024) was assigned in the SMI Security for S/MIME Module Identifier registry.
sections.eli5: Sending the short summary card to the signing box is much easier than carrying the whole heavy letter there, and the person reading can check it without holding the entire letter in their hands.

data.title: What slh_sign covers
data.code:
IF (signed attributes are absent)
THEN slh_sign(content)
ELSE signed attributes message-digest attribute = Hash(content);
     slh_sign(DER(SignedAttributes))
